name: Damon self-ligating braces
lead: Damon braces are a line of self-ligating orthodontic brackets, which hold the archwire with a built-in sliding door instead of elastic ties. They are used to align crowded or rotated teeth and to straighten the smile. The Damon SL1 was introduced in 1996 and is classed as a passive self-ligating system.[1] Manufacturers and some orthodontists say the design reduces friction and allows lighter forces, and the system is often marketed for arch expansion without extractions.

On looksmax.org, Damon braces are discussed as a way to widen the dental arch, improve the smile and, according to some posters, support jaw development. Published reviews describe a more modest picture: friction is the most consistently reported advantage in laboratory conditions, while claims about faster treatment, comfort and hygiene are mixed or unsupported.[1]

Controlled studies of the Damon system generally report that teeth align and the arches widen with treatment, and that the amount of widening is similar to that seen with conventional brackets.[6][7][8][9]
infobox: Passive self-ligating (door does not press on wire)[1]

paras: Self-ligating brackets are typically stainless steel, though ceramic and polycarbonate versions exist, and are divided into passive types, where the door applies no pressure on the wire, and active types, where a clip presses on it. Damon brackets are passive.[1] Advocates cite fewer elastic ties, a smaller appearance and shorter appointments.[1]

Passive systems aim for low friction between slot and wire, and a 2010 study cited on Wikipedia found lower static and kinetic friction for passive than active self-ligating brackets with a 0.019 by 0.025 inch stainless steel wire.[1] The Damon lineage runs from the SL1 (1996) through the Twinlock bracket by A.J. Wildman, marketed by Ormco from 1998 and later renamed Damon 2 (2000), to the Damon 3, a metal and composite hybrid introduced in 2004.[1]

The Damon system is promoted as a combined bracket and treatment approach that uses light, continuous forces with highly flexible wires and often little or no extraction. Proponents describe it as widening the arch, relieving crowding and giving a fuller smile; the 2019 systematic review of Damon philosophy tests this by comparing skeletal and dentoalveolar changes with conventional techniques.[6]

The phrase "lip bumper effect" has been used in the orthodontic literature to describe a claimed arch-widening action in which cheek and lip muscle forces are balanced by the passive bracket and flexible wires. A 2011 controlled study set out to test this claim.[9]

A 2016 meta-analysis found no hygiene or discomfort advantage for self-ligating brackets over conventional ones, and a 2016 review found no significant difference in periodontal status, according to Wikipedia's summary.[1] A 2010 review supported only shorter chair time and slightly less incisor proclination, while another analysis reported longer treatment times with self-ligating brackets.[1] A 2009 review found lower friction with small round wires in well-aligned arches but insufficient evidence for large rectangular wires.[1]

ClinicalTrials.gov lists a completed three-appliance trial (n=96, 2009 start) and a trial of Damon versus MBT brackets measuring compliance and treatment efficiency (n=34, active in 2025).[2][3] Results are not reported in the registry entries examined here. No trial examined whether Damon braces change facial structure.

A 2019 systematic review of seven controlled studies compared skeletal and dentoalveolar changes with the Damon system against conventional treatment. Most studies found an increase in maxillary intercanine, interpremolar and intermolar distance after treatment in both the Damon and comparison groups, and all concluded that the final transverse dimension did not differ significantly between them.[6]

A 2018 randomised trial in Buenos Aires treated 24 patients aged 13 to 36 with 4 to 6 mm of crowding, 12 with Damon and 12 with conventional Roth brackets, and measured dental casts after alignment. Both systems increased transverse arch diameter; the distance between upper first premolars and between canines rose more in the conventional group.[7]

A 2014 randomised comparison in 33 adolescents with Class I maxillary constriction compared Roth brackets after quad-helix expansion (17 patients) with the Damon 3MX system (16 patients). Both groups showed increased intercanine, interpremolar and intermolar widths and proclined incisors; the Damon group had a greater increase in maxillary molar inclination, and periodontal index and pain score changes did not differ.[8]

A 2011 controlled study compared 27 patients treated with the Damon system with 16 treated with conventional edgewise brackets. It found that the claimed lip bumper effect was not supported, with similar crowding relief, transverse expansion and incisor advancement in both groups.[9]

A 2014 randomised trial of 22 patients aged 16 to 30 compared gingival response in Damon and Roth brackets, and found no statistically significant difference in plaque, gingival or probing-depth indices between groups, although indices rose at 14 days, particularly with self-ligating brackets.[10] A 2016 retrospective study of 52 patients compared external apical root resorption with Damon and conventional preadjusted appliances.[11]

Forum posters often present Damon braces as preferable to conventional braces and Invisalign for arch expansion and smile aesthetics, and some link them to jaw development, nasal breathing and "mewing".[4][5] Users commonly ask whether they affect the upper jaw (maxilla), with some replies saying they allow continued growth rather than directly changing the bone.[4]

Risks are those of fixed braces generally, such as gum irritation, plaque accumulation and root resorption, and the reviewed trials do not show a hygiene or comfort difference by bracket type.[1][10][11] Case reports describe the Damon system being used in complex situations such as temporomandibular dysfunction, and studies have examined it alongside piezocision surgery, but these are not trials of facial change.[12]

timeline.event: Ormco markets the Twinlock bracket, later renamed Damon 2.[1]
Damon 3 introduced as a metal and composite hybrid.[1]

lore.intro: Looksmax.org threads describe Damon braces as the best bracket type for arch widening and facial harmony, often alongside palate expanders.[4][5]

claims.claim: Damon braces widen the dental arch better than conventional braces or Invisalign.
claims.believers: Posters say the low-friction design pushes teeth outward from both sides, improves the arch and avoids narrowing, quoting manufacturer-style descriptions.[5][4]
claims.experts: Reviews report lower friction in some wire conditions but no consistent advantage in treatment outcomes; the reviews summarised do not establish greater arch expansion.[1]

claims.claim: Damon braces improve the maxilla or shift the jaw forward.
claims.believers: One thread claims they shift the jaw forward and improve overall harmony; a reply says they let the maxilla keep developing.[5][4]
claims.experts: No published study found examining facial-skeleton change attributable to Damon brackets; bracket design is not described in the sources as altering jaw position.[1]

claims.claim: Damon braces are faster and more comfortable.
claims.believers: Posters describe them as faster and more comfortable than alternatives.[5]
claims.experts: A 2010 review supported shorter chair time only, and another analysis found longer overall treatment; a 2016 meta-analysis found no comfort advantage.[1]

claims.claim: Damon braces avoid extractions by expanding the arch.
claims.believers: Posters recommend the system for narrow arches and for avoiding extractions, often alongside palate expanders.[4][5]
claims.experts: Controlled studies report arch widening with both Damon and conventional brackets and no significant difference in final transverse dimension between them.[6][8][9]

card.summary: Passive self-ligating braces sold on low friction and arch expansion; forums rate them top, reviews find mostly mixed benefits.
card.aka: Damon System, Damon Q, self-ligating braces
card.note: No trials show facial-bone change from the bracket type.

quick.overview:
Damon braces hold the wire with a sliding door instead of rubber ties. They are marketed for lower friction, lighter forces and arch expansion.

Looksmax forums often call them the best braces for smile and arch width, but systematic reviews summarised on Wikipedia find only some benefits, chiefly lower friction and shorter chair time.
quick.mechanism: A passive clip lets the archwire slide with little pressure, so teeth move under light forces as the wire shape guides alignment.
quick.risks: Risks are those of braces generally. Reviews do not link the bracket type to extra hygiene problems or benefits; claims of jaw changes are unstudied.

chain: Passive self-ligating brackets hold the wire with a sliding door
Light, low-friction forces move teeth along the wire
Crowded teeth align and the dental arch broadens
angle.text: Damon braces straighten crowded or misaligned teeth, which changes the look of the smile directly. Orthodontists using the system describe it as expanding the arch to make room for teeth, and forum users choose it hoping for a wider smile and better facial harmony.
